direction: Residue class sieve + GPU exhaustive search for A284668(19)
rationale: Our analysis shows delay records fall in predictable residue classes mod 2^k. By pre-computing which classes have the highest guaranteed initial ascent, we can restrict an exhaustive GPU search to <1% of the search space. Barina (2025) showed GPU throughput of ~10^12 numbers/second. With sieving, searching all of [10^18, 10^19) becomes feasible on a single GPU in ~weeks.
first_step: Implement a CUDA kernel that: (1) uses a 2^16 lookup table for trailing 16 bits to skip low-delay residue classes, (2) computes compressed Collatz stopping time for surviving candidates, (3) reports any candidate with stopping time > 2283. Run on an A100 GPU.
expected_signal: Either find A284668(19) != A284668(18) (a new record exceeding 2283 steps), or confirm A284668(19) = 931386509544713451 (the 10^18 champion is also the 10^19 champion). Either result is publishable.

direction: Quantify the short-range correlation structure via 3-adic analysis
rationale: Our transition matrix analysis revealed that the compressed parity sequence deviates from i.i.d. Bernoulli in a specific way: P(1->1) = 0.366 vs expected 0.398. This ~8% deviation persists across all scales and suggests the Collatz dynamics has a 3-adic structure that creates short-range anti-correlations. The 3-adic viewpoint (expanding in powers of 3 rather than 2) may reveal this structure analytically.
first_step: Represent delay record numbers in 3-adic form. Compute the Collatz orbit in 3-adic coordinates. Measure the distribution of 3-adic digits along the orbit. Compare with the binary/parity representation. Look for patterns that explain the transition matrix deviation.
expected_signal: The 3-adic representation should reveal why P(1->1) is suppressed: two consecutive odd steps in compressed Collatz correspond to specific 3-adic constraints that reduce the probability below the i.i.d. prediction.

direction: Prove the Lyapunov critical exponent analytically
rationale: Our data shows lambda(n) ~ -C/log(n) for delay record champions, with C ~ 0.5. This logarithmic approach to criticality is reminiscent of the Berezinskii-Kosterlitz-Thouless (BKT) transition in 2D physics. If we can prove this scaling law, it would give the first rigorous bound on how slowly Collatz orbits can converge - a significant step toward the full conjecture.
first_step: Formalize the claim: for the n-th delay record d_n, prove that lambda(d_n) > -A/log(d_n) for some constant A. Use Tao's (2019) almost-all result as a starting point. The key is to show that numbers with lambda too close to 0 are 'rare' in a quantifiable sense.
expected_signal: A rigorous lower bound on |lambda| for delay records of the form |lambda| > C/log(n)^(1+epsilon) would be a genuinely new mathematical result, publishable in a top journal.

direction: Generalize to the (q,r) Collatz family and test universality
rationale: Our findings (Lyapunov criticality, transition matrix convergence, stopping time scaling) might be universal across all generalized Collatz maps T(n) = n/2 if even, (qn+r)/2 if odd. Testing this would either confirm a deep universality class or reveal that (3,1) is special. This connects to the universality concept in statistical physics.
first_step: Implement the generalized Collatz map for (q,r) = (5,1), (7,1), (3,3), (5,3). For each, find delay records up to 10^8. Compute Lyapunov exponents and transition matrices. Compare scaling exponents with (3,1).
expected_signal: If the scaling exponent alpha ~ 1.39 and the transition matrix deviations are the same across (q,r), this suggests a deep universality. If they differ, the specific values may depend on q in a predictable way (e.g., alpha ~ f(ln(2)/ln(q))).
